transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-24
Time: 14:30 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lila (Redwood SE), Jasmine (CinderLane Head of ML), Tom (Platform), Priya (CTO)

Auto-summary: weekly POC check-in focusing on cost/unit economics. Reviewed tokens-per-dollar baseline, caching impact, and batching tradeoffs. Customer provided new traffic histogram; Redwood proposed 3 tuning experiments. Agreed to run KV cache microbench, exchange price scenarios, and plan infra deep-dive for private deployment feasibility.

Topics: tokens/sec per dollar, KV cache savings, batching latency vs cost, model selection tradeoffs, security/compliance checkpoints for Private.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, appreciate it. Quick rollcall?
[00:06] Jasmine: Jasmine here. Hey.
[00:07] Tom: Tom, yep.
[00:08] Priya: Priya on.
[00:09] Lila: Lila from Redwood, hi.
[00:11] Samir: Cool. Goal today: short review of the week one metrics and then decide on next tuning experiments. We have the tokens-per-dollar baseline and some cache/ batching knobs to try.

[00:35] Jasmine: Quick note — last week we ran the integrated test and saw spikes at about 3x baseline, so curious if the batcher is hurting tail latency.
[00:42] Lila: Yeah, that matches what we saw on the telemetry. Average tokens/sec looked good but 95th latency jumped when small-burst traffic hit the batch window. We can tune batch size and max wait.

[01:05] Tom: Our priority is cost, but not at the expense of user-facing latency. For support chat we need sub-350 ms tail.
[01:14] Samir: Understood. Cost target? Last sheet showed 0.0012 tokens per dollar? sorry 1,200 tokens per dollar — I always invert that, my bad.
[01:22] Jasmine: Yeah, baseline about 1.2k tokens per dollar on hosted medium model. We want 2.5k ideally with acceptable latency tradeoffs.

[01:40] Lila: Quick framing: there are three levers — model quant/variant, batching parameters, and KV (prefix) caching. We ran a small sim: caching gave 18-42% token savings depending on hit rate.
[01:59] Priya: That 42% is optimistic, what's the hit-rate assumption?
[02:04] Lila: In that sim it was ~62% prefix reuse across sessions; realistic for our FAQ flows but less for free-form chat.
[02:12] Tom: Our traffic histogram has lots of short sessions with repeated system prompts — should help caching. I'll drop the CSV after the call.

[02:35] Samir: Great. On pricing — we can show per-token and per-embed tiers and also committed reserved capacity scenarios if you want predictable units per dollar.
[02:45] Jasmine: Does reserved capacity change the latency SLO?
[02:48] Lila: Reserved gives isolated pools so less noisy neighbors and more stable latency; for the same model it shouldn't change single-request inference time but improves 95th percentile under load.
[02:58] Samir: And financially it moves you into a committed spend but lowers effective tokens/$ by about 18% in our sample commit band.

[03:20] Jasmine: Security — we need SOC2 compliance and customer-managed KMS. Does Redwood support HSM/KMS integration for Private?
[03:29] Lila: Yes. Private supports KMS integration and we can plug in an HSM-backed key via our key provider shim; we also keep audit logs but we'll need to map retention windows.
[03:39] Priya: And SSO? We use SAML and IdP-metadata rotation.
[03:44] Samir: We support SAML/SCIM; Lila, correct on rotation?
[03:47] Lila: Yep, SAML + SCIM provisioning, and IdP cert rotation is supported — sometimes our metadata parser mangles the fingerprint name but we can walk through it in the infra call.

[04:10] Tom: Ok let's dig into the econ numbers you ran. The spreadsheet shows tokens/sec/$ for three setups — baseline hosted, hosted with caching, and dedicated reserved. Can you walk us through the assumptions?
[04:22] Lila: Sure. Baseline: hosted, default batcher, no cache. Hosted+cache: same runtime but with prefix KV cache size 4k and an assumed 45% hit rate; reserved: dedicated pool with 25% cost discount in our example and more aggressive batching (higher batch size, slightly longer max wait). We'll attach the exact request profile and tokenization assumptions.

[04:55] Jasmine: I noticed reserved + aggressive batching looked best tokens/$ but tail latency increased above our 350ms budget in the sim. Any middle ground?
[05:03] Lila: Yes — two middle grounds: keep reserved but reduce max wait to lower tail; or keep hosted with higher cache and tune batcher to favor latency (smaller batch size). We can quantify tokens/$ delta for each.

[05:28] Samir: Important note — batching improves throughput but increases per-request latency due to head-of-line wait; caching reduces token generation so reduces cost without adding latency. So caching is usually the first knob.

[05:46] Tom: In the run we saw cache evictions high. Might be our prompt variability. Lila, can you test larger prefix sizes and TTL?
[05:54] Lila: Yep — we'll try three configs: no-cache, small-prefix (2k), and large-prefix (8k) with different TTLs; measure hit rate, tokens saved, and latency change.

[06:14] Jasmine: How about model variants? We shouldn't lose quality.
[06:18] Lila: We recommend a quantized medium variant for cost and small quality delta; we'll run A/B evals on the same prompts. If quality delta is unacceptable, we fallback to slightly larger model with caching.

[06:36] Priya: Can we get a quick sanity check on throughput numbers? Our peak concurrency is ~180 req/s with average seq len 120 but 5% at 1,800 tokens.
[06:48] Samir: That outlier 5% matters a lot. For caching, the long tails can still be uncached; batching helps there but only up to a point. Lila, we'll need a workload-aware batch policy or dynamic batching.

[07:10] Lila: We have dynamic batching that adapts to traffic — it can shrink batch windows when latency spikes. We'll include that config in the microbench.

[07:22] Samir: Ok let's look at the real numbers from your test (Tom shared week1 CSV).
[07:28] Tom: Screen-shares a table — (audio) hmm the transcription may miss the table but we got these: avg tokens per call 220, median 90, long-tail 1,800 at 5%. Peak QPS at 180 for 15 minutes of the day.

[07:55] Jasmine: We want a target tokens/$ of 2.2k without exceeding 350ms p95. Can Redwood get us close?
[08:02] Lila: With caching and a medium quant, we simulated about 2.0k tokens/$ and p95 around 380ms with default batch. If we reduce batch wait and bump cache hit to 50-60% we can push toward 2.2k while hitting ~350ms p95.

[08:25] Priya: Sounds tight. What about with dedicated reserved capacity?
[08:29] Samir: Dedicated gets you lower variance and slightly better tokens/$ for heavy sustained throughput; it also gives you options to pin GPUs to model variants which reduces cold-path overhead. In our numbers dedicated + cache + tuned batch gets you to ~2.4k tokens/$ but you need the commit.

[08:50] Tom: Can we run a 48-hour microbench on dedicated? We'll need to justify commit with numbers.
[08:55] Samir: Yes, we'll run a dedicated microbench as an optional experiment — that will take ~3-4 days to schedule. Cost to Redwood is small; we'll scope exact infra in the follow-up.

[09:08] Lila: For the microbench plan: 1) baseline hosted no-cache; 2) hosted + cache (small/large prefixes); 3) hosted + dynamic batching; 4) reserved with tuned batch + cache. We'll measure tokens/$, p95 latency, and cost per 10k requests.

[09:26] Jasmine: Are there any known gotchas with cache and prompt engineering? We saw accidentally cached tokens that included ephemeral user data in one test, oops.
[09:33] Lila: Good catch — we recommend canonicalizing prompts and stripping ephemeral fields before caching. Our SDK has a preprocessor hook for that. We'll share examples.

[09:46] Tom: About observability — can we get token-level breakdowns per route and per model variant?
[09:52] Samir: Yes — Redwood Console exposes token-level dashboards (cost by route) and you can export per-route logs. We'll send a link to a sample dashboard.

[10:04] Jasmine: Any limits on cache size for Private deployments?
[10:09] Lila: Private allows you to set cache size and eviction policy; on on-prem the limit is whatever your infra supports, on our hosted there are moderate caps to avoid noisy customers. We'll detail limits in the security doc.

[10:28] Priya: Speaking of security doc — we need the exact SOC2 scope and the encryption-at-rest details.
[10:33] Samir: I'll attach SOC2 report and a KMS/HSM integration note. We'll ask security to include retention defaults and audit-log formats.

[10:45] (cross talk)
[11:00] Lila: Back to econ — small example: with cache hit 50% we saw tokens saved 34% and effective tokens/$ increased from 1.2k to 1.8k on that model. With quantization plus cache we hit ~2.2k in simulation.

[11:25] Jasmine: Could you show the per-request case where caching doesn't help?
[11:29] Lila: Sure: long session with freeform input tends to have low prefix reuse; caching only helps when the prefix (system prompt, static instructions) repeats. We'll annotate which routes benefit most.

[11:45] Tom: For our routing, can Redwood route by policy — e.g., critical payments route to dedicated and chat to hosted?
[11:52] Samir: Yes that's smart. Smart routing can send high-priority traffic to reserved pools and keep bulk chat on hosted to save money. We'll include a proposed routing policy example.

[12:05] Priya: Any regulatory or residency constraints? We're US-only for now but healthcare PII is in scope for a later phase.
[12:12] Lila: For healthcare we'll recommend Private with VPC peering and KMS — we also support HIPAA addendum in Private agreements.

[12:26] Jasmine: Ok let's get concrete: run the three cache configs and the dynamic batch test next week and share numbers. Also send pricing scenarios (hosted vs reserved) that include projected tokens/$ at our expected traffic.
[12:37] Samir: Agreed. Lila you'll lead the bench.
[12:40] Lila: Yep. We'll post a single spreadsheet with tabs for each experiment and the raw logs.

[12:50] (background noise — someone typing)
[13:05] Samir: Quick Q — competitors: Jasmine asked about Anthropic; their pricing model looked simpler for small teams but their throughput at long sequences wasn't as cost-efficient in our bench. We'll include a brief competitor note.

[13:20] Jasmine: Thanks. Also please call out differences in tokenization assumptions; we saw 3-4% variance across tokenizers.
[13:27] Lila: Will do.

[13:35] Samir: Alright let's capture action items and close.
[13:40] (summary)
[13:42] Samir: Summary: run cache experiments (no, 2k, 8k), dynamic batching microbench, optionally schedule 48hr dedicated bench. Price scenarios + SOC2/KMS docs to be sent.
[13:55] Jasmine: Sounds good.
[13:58] Tom: Thanks everyone.
[14:00] Priya: Thanks.
